### Introduce yourself

I use scikit-learn for general ML work. I found this while cross-checking
the `PolynomialCountSketch` docs against its implementation for an unrelated
performance PR (#34919) and noticed the `bitHash_` attribute's documented
dtype doesn't match what the code actually produces.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`PolynomialCountSketch`'s `bitHash_` attribute is documented as:

```
bitHash_ : ndarray of shape (degree, n_features), dtype=float32
    Array with random entries in {+1, -1}, used to represent
    the 2-wise independent hash functions for Count Sketch computation.
```

but it is actually set with:

```python
self.bitHash_ = random_state.choice(a=[-1, 1], size=(self.degree, n_features))
```

`numpy.random.RandomState.choice` with an integer array `a=[-1, 1]` and no
explicit `dtype` produces an integer array, not `float32`. This has been the
case since the class was introduced (scikit-learn/scikit-learn#13003, 2019),
so it is not a regression, just a docstring that was never accurate.

User-facing impact is limited (the attribute is internal-ish and the class
still works correctly), but anyone relying on the documented dtype — for
example writing code that assumes `bitHash_.astype(np.float32, copy=False)`
is a no-op, or reasoning about memory usage from the docstring — would be
misled.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.kernel_approximation import PolynomialCountSketch

X = np.random.RandomState(0).random_sample((50, 20))
ps = PolynomialCountSketch(degree=2, n_components=10, random_state=0).fit(X)
print(ps.bitHash_.dtype)
```

### Expected Results

```
float32
```
(matching the docstring)

### Actual Results

```
int64
```

The `X` parameter description in `MaxAbsScaler.partial_fit()` currently states that the data is used to compute the **"per-feature minimum and maximum"**.

```

I believe this is a documentation-only issue and does not require any change to the underlying algorithm.

```text
The data used to compute the per-feature minimum and maximum
used for later scaling along the features axis.
```

to:

```text
The data used to compute the per-feature maximum absolute value

Investigation: conda-forge scikit-learn slower than PyPI (ExtraTrees case)

While looking at [builds comparison results](https://probabl-ai.github.io/scikit-learn-benchmarks/builds_comparison.html) from my benchmarks (https://github.com/probabl-ai/scikit-learn-benchmarks), I noticed `ExtraTrees*.fit` was often ~25% slower on conda-forge builds of
scikit-learn 1.9.0 than on PyPI wheels.

Two distinct bugs were found along the way; only the second one explains the slowdown:

1. **O3 vs O2** (documented in #34865): `-O3` in meson doesn't survive an environment `CFLAGS` that also sets `-O2` (which conda-forge's compiler activation does).

2. **Version of `glibc`** (cause of the slowdown): conda-forge compiles scikit-learn against a `sysroot_linux-64=2.17` (glibc 2.17, from 2012-12-25). That old glibc's `<math.h>` defines the `isnan()` macro as a dispatch to glibc-internal `__isnanf`/`__isnan` functions instead of `__builtin_isnan*`. GCC can't recognize or inline those, so `sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx`'s `isnan(value)` calls — sitting in the hottest loop of tree-building (`find_min_max`, `partition_samples`) — become genuine non-inlined function calls. This is `fit`-specific (confirmed: `predict`, which doesn't call these functions, shows no slowdown) and fully reproduced from source once the exact sysroot was pinned.


This is very likely **not scikit-learn-specific**: any conda-forge package with a hot-loop `isnan()`/`isinf()` call is plausibly exposed the same way.

### Proposed fix

Replace `from libc.math cimport isnan` / `isnan(value)` in `sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx` and `sklearn/tree/_utils.pxd` (and any other tree/HGB hot loop doing the same) with the self-inequality NaN test `value != value`. Pure comparison, nothing to inline, immune to this class of bug on any compiler/libc, forever.

### Root cause, in detail

*(pure LLM write-up)*

<details>

`sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx` (`DensePartitioner.find_min_max`, `.partition_samples`) and `sklearn/tree/_utils.pxd` call `isnan(value)` on `float32_t` data, via `from libc.math cimport isnan`. This runs once per sample per feature scan during `fit`; never during `predict`.

The feedstock's CI pin file (`.ci_support/linux_64_python3.12.____cpython.yaml` at the 1.9.0 release commit) sets `c_stdlib: sysroot`, `c_stdlib_version: '2.17'`. That sysroot's `math.h` has:

```c
#  define isnan(x) \
     (sizeof (x) == sizeof (float) ? __isnanf (x) \
      : sizeof (x) == sizeof (double) ? __isnan (x) : __isnanl (x))
```

Once the preprocessor expands this, the identifier `isnan` is gone from
the translation unit — GCC has nothing left to recognize as a builtin, so
`__isnanf` (an ordinary external glibc symbol, not a compiler intrinsic)
gets a real out-of-line call. Modern glibc instead defines `isnan(x)` as
`__builtin_isnan(x)` directly, which GCC folds to 2 instructions
(`ucomiss`/`setp`). PyPI/manylinux wheels don't hit this because they're
built with devtoolset-style toolchains: modern compiler *and* modern
headers, achieving old-system compatibility via glibc *symbol versioning*
at link time rather than by literally compiling against old headers.

Confirmed end to end:
- `perf`-profiled real installed PyPI vs conda-forge packages
  (`ExtraTreesRegressor.fit`, `n_features=30`): conda-forge spends 12.6% of
  samples in `__isnanf` alone; PyPI doesn't show it in the top 15 at all.
- Disassembled both real `.so` files directly: conda-forge's
  `find_min_max` has `call *0x1791f(%rip)  # <__isnanf@GLIBC_2.2.5>`;
  PyPI's has no call at all.
- Reproduced from source: rebuilding the actual v1.9.0 tag with the exact
  matching GCC (14.3.0-19, confirmed via the real binary's own
  `.comment` section) reproduced nothing *until* `sysroot_linux-64=2.17`
  was pinned explicitly (every environment had otherwise resolved the
  latest default, 2.39) — at which point the non-inlined call and the
  larger function size reappeared byte-for-byte.
- Same `isnan()` call pattern, same functions, confirmed still present on
  current `main` (the categorical-feature/Breiman-shortcut work added
  since 1.9.0 didn't touch this code path — `find_min_max` compiles to the
  identical byte size on both).

</details>

### Everything else that was tried and ruled out

Before finding the sysroot, a long list of variables was controlled for one at a time and **did not** reproduce the real-world gap when rebuilding from source with the real conda-forge `gcc_linux-64`/`gxx_linux-64` toolchain:

<details>

- `-O2` vs `-O3` in isolation (~1.7% effect — this is the Meson bug above)
- `-march=nocona -mtune=haswell` vs no override
- GCC version: 16.2.0, 13.4.0, and the exact `14.3.0-19` patch build
  (pinning `gcc_impl_linux-64`/`gxx_impl_linux-64`/`binutils_impl_linux-64`
  precisely, since `gcc_impl_linux-64` has its own build-number sequence
  independent of the `gcc_linux-64` wrapper)
- Cython version (real binary uses 3.2.5; early rebuilds had picked up
  3.3.0 by default — controlled for, no effect)
- Exact v1.9.0 source tag vs current `main`
- Editable install vs literal `python -m build -w` wheel build (matching
  `build.sh` exactly)
- `-fno-merge-constants` (the extra flag conda-forge adds under
  `CONDA_BUILD=1`)
- joblib version, core-count detection, BLAS threading config — all
  identical between real PyPI and conda-forge installs

</details>

Yes, I'll open the PR very soon.

OneHotEncoder unknown-category warning is incorrect for columns without an infrequent category

### Introduce yourself

I'm learning ML engineering and use scikit-learn for a delay-prediction model on
US flight data. This is the first issue I've opened. I encountered this while working out how to encode categorical columns that may contain previously unseen values during prediction.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Carrier and destination can't be enumerated ahead of time, so both go to one
encoder with `drop="first"`, `handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"` and
`min_frequency=4`. On my first CV fold, 41,901 rows, it fits to:

```
infrequent_categories_: [None, array(['HDN'], dtype=object)]
```

Destination gets an infrequent bucket. Carrier gets `None` because its rarest value has 148 rows in that fold and 744 across the training pool, so it is not below `min_frequency=4`. Transforming a row with an unknown carrier and an unknown destination produces this warning:

```
Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. These unknown
categories will be encoded as the infrequent category.
```

The warning claims that the unknown categories in both columns will go to the infrequent category, but this is not true for the carrier feature because no `infrequent_sklearn` column exists for it, and the transformed row is zero across the entire carrier block.

This matters because `drop="first"` drops the encoded feature for the first carrier category (`AA` in this fold), making all zeros its carrier encoding. An unknown airline and a real flight belonging to `AA` therefore produce an identical carrier encoding, so the model treats them the same with respect to the carrier feature.

I caught this by inspecting `infrequent_categories_`, transforming a row containing an unknown carrier and destination, and comparing the resulting vector with `get_feature_names_out()`. The carrier block was entirely zero, even though the warning said that the unknown carrier would be encoded as the infrequent category. The warning should have identified that the unknown carrier was encoded as all zeros, while the unknown destination was routed to its infrequent bucket.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import warnings

from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

# Column 0: "a" and "b" both appear twice, so it has no infrequent category.
# Column 1: "y" appears once, so it does have an infrequent category.
X = [["a", "x"], ["a", "x"], ["b", "x"], ["b", "y"]]

encoder = OneHotEncoder(
    drop="first",
    sparse_output=False,
    handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist",
    min_frequency=2,
).fit(X)

print("infrequent_categories_:", encoder.infrequent_categories_)
print("feature names:         ", encoder.get_feature_names_out())

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    X_trans = encoder.transform([["c", "z"]])

print("transform([['c', 'z']]):", X_trans)
print("warning:", caught[0].message)
```

Both columns receive an unknown category, but only column 1 has an infrequent
category that can absorb it.


### Expected Results

The warning should describe what actually happens to each column. Column 1 has
an infrequent category, so its unknown value is encoded there. Column 0 has
no infrequent category, so its unknown value is encoded as all zeros, which is the same encoding `drop="first"` assigns to the dropped category.

Something along the lines of:

```
Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. The unknown
categories in columns [1] will be encoded as the infrequent category. Those in
columns [0] will be encoded as all zeros, because these columns have no
infrequent category.
```

This is also what the `handle_unknown` docstring already documents:

> If the `'infrequent'` category does not exist, then `transform` and
> `inverse_transform` will handle an unknown category as with
> `handle_unknown='ignore'`.


### Actual Results

```
infrequent_categories_: [None, array(['y'], dtype=object)]
feature names:          ['x0_b' 'x1_infrequent_sklearn']
transform([['c', 'z']]): [[0. 1.]]
warning: Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. These unknown categories will be encoded as the infrequent category.
```

No exception is raised. The problem is that the warning talks about both columns and
makes a single claim about them, which is false for column 0: its
`infrequent_categories_` entry is `None`, no `x0_infrequent_sklearn` column
exists in `get_feature_names_out()`, and the transformed row is `0` across the

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation



When `max_categories` forces additional categories into the infrequent group beyond what `min_frequency` alone would select, and multiple categories are tied in count at the cutoff boundary, the docs for `max_categories` don't specify which tied category is kept as frequent vs. grouped as infrequent.

Looking at `_identify_infrequent()` in `sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py`, the tie-break is implicit rather than documented:

```python
# stable sort to preserve original count order
smallest_levels = np.argsort(category_count, kind="mergesort")[:-frequent_category_count]
infrequent_mask[smallest_levels] = True
```

Counts are sorted using `np.argsort(category_count, kind="mergesort")` — a stable sort — so ties are resolved by the order categories appear in `categories_[i]`, which for `categories='auto'` is lexicographic/numeric sort order. This behavior is not mentioned in the `max_categories` docstring or the User Guide section on infrequent categories (`encoder_infrequent_categories`).

### Suggest a potential alternative/fix

Add a sentence to the `max_categories` parameter docs (in both `OneHotEncoder` and `OrdinalEncoder`) and to the User Guide section on infrequent categories, stating that ties in category count are broken using the sort order of the categories (via a stable sort). This is also relevant to the discussion in #32161.

### Minimal reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

X = np.array([["a"] * 2 + ["b"] * 2 + ["c"] * 5], dtype=object).T
enc = OneHotEncoder(max_categories=2, sparse_output=False).fit(X)
print(enc.infrequent_categories_)
# 'a' and 'b' tie at count=2 -- which one is grouped as infrequent
# is not documented, though it is deterministic.
```

Related: #32161 discusses tie-breaking by lexicographical order for encoder category ordering more broadly.

`UnionFind.fast_find`'s path compression never touches the queried node — quadratic linkage labelling

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`UnionFind.fast_find`'s path-compression loop never actually shortens the path of the node it was called on, so path compression is effectively disabled. `fast_find` degenerates to a plain, uncompressed find. Callers that build a dendrogram (e.g. `make_single_linkage`) allocate a new parent node per merge, so single-linkage/chaining inputs produce O(n)-deep union-find trees; with compression disabled, the repeated uncompressed finds sum to **O(n²)**. This is invisible on small inputs but dominates end-to-end runtime at scale (tens of seconds at n≈200k in a comparable reproduction — see the linked hdbscan report for measured numbers against the same code pattern).

**File:** `sklearn/cluster/_hierarchical_fast.pyx` — `UnionFind.fast_find`
**Also affects:** `sklearn/cluster/_hdbscan/_linkage.pyx::make_single_linkage`, which calls `UnionFind.fast_find` in its inner loop; and, within `sklearn/cluster/_agglomerative.py`, `AgglomerativeClustering(linkage="single")` / `FeatureAgglomeration(linkage="single")`, both of which route through `_hierarchical.single_linkage_label` / `_hierarchical._single_linkage_label` (the unconstrained and connectivity-constrained paths, respectively) in `linkage_tree()`. Other linkages (`ward`, `average`, `complete`) use a separate heap + `IntFloatDict` implementation and are **not** affected.
**Type:** performance (results are correct; time is quadratic)
**Related:** the same defect exists independently in the `hdbscan` package (`scikit-learn-contrib/hdbscan`, `hdbscan/_hdbscan_linkage.pyx`), which has its own vendored copy of this `UnionFind`. Bug report: [https://github.com/scikit-learn-contrib/hdbscan/issues/731](https://github.com/scikit-learn-contrib/hdbscan/issues/731).
**LLM usage**: found using Claude, reviewed manually.

    rows = []
    w = 0
    for i in range(K - 1):

### Interest in fixing the bug

## The code

```cython
# sklearn/cluster/_hierarchical_fast.pyx
cdef class UnionFind(object):

    def __init__(self, N):
        self.parent = np.full(2 * N - 1, -1., dtype=np.intp, order='C')
        self.next_label = N
        self.size = np.hstack((np.ones(N, dtype=np.intp),
                               np.zeros(N - 1, dtype=np.intp)))

    cdef void union(self, intp_t m, intp_t n) noexcept:
        self.parent[m] = self.next_label
        self.parent[n] = self.next_label
        self.size[self.next_label] = self.size[m] + self.size[n]
        self.next_label += 1
        return

    @cython.wraparound(True)
    cdef intp_t fast_find(self, intp_t n) noexcept:
        cdef intp_t p
        p = n
        # find the highest node in the linkage graph so far
        while self.parent[n] != -1:
            n = self.parent[n]
        # provide a shortcut up to the highest node
        while self.parent[p] != n:
            p, self.parent[p] = self.parent[p], n
        return n
```

## Root cause

The "shortcut" line

```cython
p, self.parent[p] = self.parent[p], n
```

is a chained tuple assignment `target1, target2 = rhs1, rhs2`. Cython (like Python) evaluates the full right-hand side first — as a tuple, using the *current* value of `p` — and only then performs the assignments, **left to
right**:

1. Evaluate `rhs = (self.parent[p], n)` using the old `p`.
2. Assign target 1: `p = rhs[0]` — `p` is rebound *now*, to its old parent.
3. Assign target 2: `self.parent[p] = rhs[1]` — but this indexes with the **already-updated** `p` from step 2, not the node the loop meant to compress. The write lands one hop up from where it was intended.

The node originally passed to `fast_find(n)` is therefore never repointed at the root; only its ancestors shift by one hop per call. Reproducing the assignment in isolation:

```python
>>> parent = [1, 2, 3, -1]          # chain 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3(root)
>>> p, n = 0, 3
>>> p, parent[p] = parent[p], n     # one iteration of the "compression" loop
>>> p, parent
(1, [1, 3, 3, -1])                  # node 0 STILL points at 1 — untouched
```

Every subsequent `fast_find(0)` re-walks `0 → 1 → 3`, and this compounds across the whole tree, producing the O(n²) behavior.

## Impact

- Any caller that builds a chained union-find structure and repeatedly calls `fast_find` on it is quadratic in the number of points, dominated by re-walked, uncompressed paths. This includes `make_single_linkage` in `sklearn/cluster/_hdbscan/_linkage.pyx` (used by HDBSCAN) and `AgglomerativeClustering(linkage="single")` /
  `FeatureAgglomeration(linkage="single")` in `sklearn/cluster/_agglomerative.py`.
- **Results are unaffected.** `fast_find` still returns the correct root (the outer `while self.parent[n] != -1` loop correctly finds it), so linkage/hierarchy output is unchanged; this is purely a performance bug.

## Suggested fix

Walk to the root first, then compress every node on the path in a second pass. This sidesteps the tuple-assignment aliasing trap entirely:

```cython
cdef intp_t fast_find(self, intp_t n) noexcept:
    cdef intp_t root, nxt
    root = n
    while self.parent[root] != -1:
        root = self.parent[root]
    while self.parent[n] != -1 and self.parent[n] != root:
        nxt = self.parent[n]
        self.parent[n] = root
        n = nxt
    return root
```

Roots are unchanged, so output is bit-identical; only the amortized complexity of repeated `fast_find` calls improves (from effectively uncompressed to near-inverse-Ackermann with compression restored).

## Notes

- See the companion `hdbscan` package report (linked at the top of this file) for a worked measurement of the same pattern in a near-identical (ndarray-backed, rather than memoryview-backed) `UnionFind`.

### Proposed Example / Documentation Improvement
I would like to propose a new gallery example focused on evaluating Precision-Recall curves on highly imbalanced financial datasets (e.g., payment fraud detection).

### Motivation & Context
In production settings like FinTech, target classes are highly imbalanced (~1-2% positive class), making PR-AUC and threshold tuning critical compared to standard ROC-AUC metrics. 

While docstrings focus strictly on minimal syntax, having a dedicated application example in the User Guide gallery will help practitioners:
1. Compare ROC vs. Precision-Recall curves on imbalanced distributions.
2. Demonstrate threshold selection strategies for high-precision vs. high-recall trade-offs in fraud context.

- Dataset generation / loading simulating payment fraud class ratios (`make_classification` or synthetic imbalance).
- Fitting baseline models (e.g., Logistic Regression / Tree-based).
- Plotting Precision-Recall vs. ROC curves side-by-side using `PrecisionRecallDisplay`.

OneHotEncoder: inverse_transform decodes unknown categories as the dropped category (not None) when drop + handle_unknown='ignore'

### Describe the bug

When `OneHotEncoder` is configured with both `drop='first'` (or any `drop`) and
`handle_unknown='ignore'`, unknown categories are silently decoded as the
**dropped** category by `inverse_transform`, instead of `None`.

This directly contradicts the documented behavior of `handle_unknown='ignore'`.
The parameter docstring states:

> 'ignore' : When an unknown category is encountered during transform, the
> resulting one-hot encoded columns for this feature will be all zeros. **In the
> inverse transform, an unknown category will be denoted as None.**

The root cause is an unavoidable encoding collision: the dropped category and an
unknown category are **both** encoded as the all-zeros vector, so they are
indistinguishable at `inverse_transform` time. The current implementation
resolves the ambiguity in favor of the dropped category
(`sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py`, `inverse_transform`), which means a
round-trip silently rewrites unknown values into a valid, known category with no
warning.

Note there is also an internal documentation inconsistency: the `handle_unknown`
parameter docstring promises `None`, while the `inverse_transform` method
docstring says the dropped category is used. The two contradict each other.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

ohe = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="first", sparse_output=False)
ohe.fit(np.array([["a"], ["b"], ["c"]]))

X = np.array([["a"], ["b"], ["c"], ["z"]])   # "z" is unknown
encoded = ohe.transform(X)
back = ohe.inverse_transform(encoded)

print("dropped category 'a' ->", ohe.transform([["a"]]))   # [[0. 0.]]
print("unknown   'z'      ->", ohe.transform([["z"]]))      # [[0. 0.]]  (identical!)
print("round-trip:", back.ravel().tolist())
```

### Expected Results

Per the `handle_unknown='ignore'` documentation, the unknown value should be
decoded as `None`:

```
['a', 'b', 'c', None]
```

### Actual Results

The unknown value is silently decoded as the dropped category `'a'`:

```
['a', 'b', 'c', 'a']
```

The dropped category and the unknown category produce the identical all-zeros
encoding `[[0. 0.]]`, so they cannot be told apart on inverse transform, and the
unknown is silently turned into a real category.

### Impact

`inverse_transform(transform(X))` is not a safe round trip when `drop` and
`handle_unknown='ignore'` are combined: unknown/invalid inputs are silently
converted into a valid known category, with no warning. This is an easy
data-integrity footgun in preprocessing pipelines.

### Possible resolutions

Some options for discussion:

1. Fix the `handle_unknown` docstring to explicitly document that when `drop` is
   set, unknown categories are decoded as the dropped category (documentation
   only), and reconcile it with the `inverse_transform` docstring.
2. Emit a warning from `inverse_transform` when the ambiguous `drop` +
   `handle_unknown='ignore'` combination causes all-zero rows to be decoded as
   the dropped category.
3. Consider disallowing / warning on the ambiguous `drop` +
   `handle_unknown='ignore'` combination at `fit` time.

Happy to open a PR once maintainers indicate the preferred direction.

### Versions

```

    Python 3.11.9
Python dependencies:
    scikit-learn: 1.9.0
    numpy:        2.4.6
    scipy:        1.17.1
```

Behavior also confirmed by source inspection on `main`
(`sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py`, `handle_unknown` docstring vs.
`inverse_transform`).

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When passing a Pandas `DataFrame` containing modern nullable extension dtypes (such as `Int64` or `Float64`) with missing values (`pd.NA`) into `PowerTransformer`, the estimator crashes with an unhandled internal exception (`TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous`) rather than coercing the array cleanly or raising a standard scikit-learn `ValueError`.

### Context & User-Facing Impact

1. **Modern Pandas Integration:** With modern Pandas workflows (including Pandas 2.0+ defaults and `df.convert_dtypes()`), nullable integer and float types are standard when working with tabular data that contains missing values. 
2. **Pipeline Failures:** In production data pipelines, passing a DataFrame with nullable dtypes directly into a scikit-learn `Pipeline([('power_transform', PowerTransformer()), ...])` causes the entire pipeline to fail with a low-level Pandas boolean evaluation error instead of processing the data smoothly.
3. **Unnecessary Workarounds:** To bypass this bug, users currently have to manually write boilerplate pre-casting logic (e.g., `df.astype("float64")`) before calling `PowerTransformer`, which breaks scikit-learn's native DataFrame compatibility goals.
4. **Consistency:** Most scikit-learn estimators handle Pandas extension arrays seamlessly by converting them to standard floating-point NumPy arrays via `_validate_data`. `PowerTransformer` should follow this same pattern.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer

# Minimal DataFrame using Pandas nullable integer extension dtype ('Int64')
# The missing value (None) is automatically represented as pd.NA
X = pd.DataFrame({"col": pd.Series([1, 2, None, 4], dtype="Int64")})

# Triggers raw TypeError inside PowerTransformer during internal array checks
pt = PowerTransformer(method="box-cox")
pt.fit_transform(X)

`PowerTransformer` should automatically coerce Pandas nullable extension arrays into standard IEEE floating-point NumPy arrays (`np.float64` or `np.float32`) via `_validate_data` before evaluating numerical bound checks.

Specifically:
- It should not crash with a raw `TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous`.
- Passing data with nullable dtypes should either complete successfully (coercing `pd.NA` to `np.nan`) or raise a clear, standardized `ValueError` if input constraints are violated.

### Actual Results

The estimator crashes with a raw `TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous` during internal positivity checks (`X <= 0`):

Inconsistent `_check_initialized` method: only present on gradient boosting estimators

While reviewing #34495, I noticed that `_check_initialized` only exists on the gradient boosting estimators and nowhere else in the codebase. The method does nothing but wrap `check_is_fitted(self)`.

## Steps to reproduce
```
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    AdaBoostClassifier,
    GradientBoostingClassifier,
    GradientBoostingRegressor,
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    RandomForestClassifier,
)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

estimators = [
    GradientBoostingClassifier(),
    GradientBoostingRegressor(),
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier(),
    AdaBoostClassifier(),
    RandomForestClassifier(),
    LogisticRegression(),
]

for est in estimators:
    print(f"{type(est).__name__:32s} _check_initialized? {hasattr(est, '_check_initialized')}")
```

## Results
```
GradientBoostingClassifier       _check_initialized? True
GradientBoostingRegressor        _check_initialized? True
HistGradientBoostingClassifier   _check_initialized? False
AdaBoostClassifier               _check_initialized? False
RandomForestClassifier           _check_initialized? False
LogisticRegression               _check_initialized? False
```

## Background
I tried to trace how the method was introduced. As far as I can tell it first appeared in 2015 and was never explicitly discussed — the surrounding conversations are all about the apply method. Please correct me if I've missed something:
- 2015: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/5228
- 2016: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/7464
- 2019: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/14545

## Questions
1. Should `_check_initialized` be generalized across the other estimators — e.g. moved up into `BaseEnsemble`?

Pandas output path fails to reject infinite values during transform

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When using `set_output(transform="pandas")`, `SelectKBest.transform` does not reject infinite values in a pandas `DataFrame`. This is a regression introduced by [PR #25102](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/25102).

The pandas-output path passes `cast_to_ndarray=False` to `_validate_data`, which causes `check_array` to skip its `force_all_finite` validation. This allows invalid numeric inputs through `transform` instead of raising the expected validation error.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif

X_train = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "a": [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0],
        "b": [1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 2.0],
    }
)
y = [0, 0, 1, 1]

selector = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=1).set_output(transform="pandas")
selector.fit(X_train, y)

X_bad = X_train.copy()
X_bad.loc[0, "a"] = np.inf

print("Input containing infinity:")
print(X_bad)
print()

try:
    result = selector.transform(X_bad)
    print("Transform succeeded (no error raised):")
    print(result)
except Exception as exc:
    print("Error:", exc)
```

### Expected Results

The input containing infinity should be rejected during `transform`:

```
Input containing infinity:
     a    b
0  inf  1.0
1  1.0  2.0
2  0.0  1.0
3  1.0  2.0

Error: Input X contains infinity or a value too large for dtype('float64').
```

(This is the behavior when `set_output` is not used.)

### Actual Results

No validation error is raised; transform silently succeeds:

```
Input containing infinity:
     a    b
0  inf  1.0
1  1.0  2.0
2  0.0  1.0
3  1.0  2.0

Transform succeeded (no error raised):
     b
0  1.0
1  2.0
2  1.0
3  2.0
```

### Versions

```
scikit-learn 1.9.0
Python 3.11.13
Linux
NumPy 2.4.6
SciPy 1.17.1
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

The pandas-output path should preserve DataFrame containers without changing the estimator's validation behavior. Infinite values should continue to be rejected consistently during `transform` regardless of the output format setting.

Found this while poking around _gb.py. _resize_state has a check meant to give a clear error if you try to shrink n_estimators:

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When `radius` is passed as a per-sample array, `NearestNeighbors.radius_neighbors` returns a correct result with `n_jobs=1` but raises a `ValueError` with `n_jobs>1` on identical input for both `ball_tree` and `kd_tree`. An `n_jobs` value should not change behavior.

`NearestNeighbors` is a convenient interface to `BallTree` and `KDTree` because, unlike those, it accepts an `n_jobs` parameter.

I used the following workaround in the past, [here](https://github.com/nicolassalvy/ClippedDensityCoverage/blob/main/ClippedDensityCoverage/metrics/Clipped_Density_Coverage.py#L52-71):
```python
tree = NearestNeighbors(
    algorithm="ball_tree", n_jobs=n_jobs
).fit(data1)

distances, indices = (
    tree.radius_neighbors(
        X=data2,
        radius=np.max(radii),
        return_distance=True,
        sort_results=False,
    )
)

correct_indices = [
    indices[i][distances[i] <= radii[i]]
    for i in range(len(distances))
]
```
but this can be very slow, both because of the mandatory `return_distance=True` and because of the following: adaptive radius search is useful here because the typical distances in different data modes can be very different, one mode where they are very far apart and another where they are close. With the workaround, the indices returned for half the data could be that whole half every time, which makes the results very slow.

A related feature request showed interest: [#25970](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/25970) ("Allow NearestNeighbor radius_neighbors to accept an array for the `radius` keyword argument"), though this present issue is only about the tree-based algorithms, which already accept it at `n_jobs=1` and only break under parallelism, not the `brute`-force case.

from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

`CalibratedClassifierCV(method="sigmoid")` should always take the raw logits as inputs instead of the predicted probabilities This is a defect [I first observed while reviewing the temperature scaling PR](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31068#discussion_r2012459507): if the uncalibrated classifier only exposes a `decision_function` and no `predict_proba` (which is the case for SVMs for instance) our implementation of sigmoid calibration (aka Platt-scaling) is fine because the output values of `decision_function` are morally logits between -inf and +inf with 0 as the default decision threshold. But if the uncalibrated classifier already exposes a `predict_proba` method (e.g. `GaussianNB`), our current implementation takes the predicted probabilities as input of the parametrized sigmoid function. This is incorrect: we should the log of the probabilistic predictions (incremented by a small epsilon) to feed logits as inputs to the sigmoid function. Using `move_to` on a numpy array with negative stride crashes the Python process

The `move_to` function we have for moving arrays from one namespace to another can crash the Python process when you ask it to move an array with negative strides. I found this while working on `PCA` where we have an array with negative stride (`Vt` from `_fit_truncated`).

The code below is a reproducer:

```python
import numpy as np
import torch
import sklearn
from sklearn.utils._array_api import get_namespace_and_device, move_to

def make_negative_strided():
    """A small, contiguous-source array viewed with a negative stride."""
    a = np.arange(12.0).reshape(3, 4)[:, ::-1]
    assert not a.flags["C_CONTIGUOUS"]
    assert a.strides[-1] < 0
    return a

a = make_negative_strided()
with sklearn.config_context(array_api_dispatch=True):
    xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(torch.asarray([1.0]))
    try:
        move_to(a, xp=xp, device=device)
    except Exception as exc:  # it is not caught
        print("Caught a Python exception (unexpected):", type(exc).__name__, exc)
    else:
        # this doesn't happen
        print("move_to returned without error (unexpected)")

    # instead the process exits with a SIGABRT
```

AI tells me that a possible fix is to call `np.ascontiguousarray(array)` if the input `array` is an array with negative stride. In addition we should [only apply this workaround in the case where the `move_to` target is torch](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34307#issuecomment-4778962780). The comment for the workaround should also include a link to https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/188023 and this issue so we can know when the work around can be removed.

Something like this, but with a check for torch as target:
```diff
--- a/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py
+++ b/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py
@@ def move_to(*arrays, xp, device):
             xp_array, _, device_array = get_namespace_and_device(array)
             if xp == xp_array and device == device_array:
                 converted_arrays.append(array)
             else:
+                strides = getattr(array, "strides", None)
+                if strides is not None and any(
+                    stride < 0 for stride in strides
+                ):
+                    # Some libraries (e.g. torch) do not raise a catchable
+                    # Python exception but abort the whole process when a NumPy
+                    # array with negative or zero strides is imported via DLPack
+                    # (such arrays are produced for instance by ``a[::-1]``
+                    # reversals, as done by ARPACK). The ``except`` clause below
+                    # therefore cannot protect against it, so the source array is
+                    # made contiguous first to guarantee positive strides.
+                    array = numpy.ascontiguousarray(array)
                 try:
                     # The dlpack protocol is the future proof and library agnostic
                     # method to transfer arrays across namespace and device boundaries
                     # hence this method is attempted first and going through NumPy is
                     # only used as fallback in case of failure.
                     # Note: copy=None is the default since array-api 2023.12. Namespace
                     # libraries should only trigger a copy automatically if needed.
                     array_converted = xp.from_dlpack(array, device=device)
```

What do others think about this? I am also wondering if this is a bug in numpy's DLPack implementation (should not expose arrays with negative stride) or if this is a bug in torch (should check for negative stride before doing anything)?

I think that `numpy.ascontiguousarray(array)` is free for most arrays, those that already full fill it. For arrays that are not already contiguous I don't know what the cost is, but I think there is no alternative?

RFC Automatically close pull requests linked to issues that are not ready for contributions

Disclosure: I used LLM to proofread earlier drafts of this issue. All mistakes are due to me.

TL;DR: This RFC discusses whether pull requests linked to issues not yet ready for contributions should be automatically closed to reduce repetitive reviewer workload.

### The Situation

In the current review workflow, reviewers typically start with the following steps before inspecting the changes:

1. Manually check whether the pull request is linked to an issue that is ready for contributions (e.g., not labelled "Needs Triage").
2. If the linked issue is not yet ready for a pull request, reviewers need to explain this to the author and then close the pull request.

While this process is straightforward and the decision-making is usually quick, it can become repetitive over time and contribute to reviewer fatigue, increasing the maintenance burden.

#33521 reduces the time needed for step 1. However, explaining to contributors why a pull request is being closed because the linked issue is not ready (including wording and tone) is still time-consuming, and is often repeated in very similar forms. See https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/32951#pullrequestreview-3613580879, https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33455#pullrequestreview-3894730435, and https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33695#pullrequestreview-4060391909 for examples.

### Proposed Solution

During the 2026 sprint, we (@AnneBeyer, @StefanieSenger, and myself) discussed mitigating step 2 by introducing a bot that automatically closes pull requests linked to issues that are not yet ready for contributions. This builds on #33521, and is relatively straightforward from a technical standpoint.

However, the proposed approach has at least two potential concerns:

1. It may close pull requests that are intended as PoC for issues still under discussion, such as #34242.
2. It may introduce security considerations (e.g., GitHub token handling).

Despite these concerns, we believe this RFC could help address these issues and improve the overall review experience in the long run.

DOC: inconsistent monotonic_cst docstring across forest estimators

### Describe the issue linked to the documentation

### Describe the issue

In `sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py`, the `monotonic_cst` parameter docstring 
has two inconsistencies across the forest estimators:

**1. Missing trailing comma in shape notation**

All four classes (`RandomForestClassifier`, `RandomForestRegressor`, 
`ExtraTreesClassifier`, `ExtraTreesRegressor`) write the shape as:

    array-like of int of shape (n_features)

It should be:

    array-like of int of shape (n_features,)

This is inconsistent with the rest of the scikit-learn codebase which 
uses the trailing comma to denote a 1D tuple.

**2. Inconsistent wording for constraint values**

`RandomForestClassifier` uses:
    - 1: monotonic increase
    - -1: monotonic decrease

While `RandomForestRegressor`, `ExtraTreesClassifier`, and 
`ExtraTreesRegressor` use:
    - 1: monotonically increasing
    - -1: monotonically decreasing

Both should use the same phrasing. The adjective form 
("monotonically increasing/decreasing") is more grammatically 
consistent with how constraints are described elsewhere.

### Steps to reproduce

Open `sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py` and search for `monotonic_cst`.

### Suggested fix

- Add trailing comma: `(n_features,)` in all four classes
- Standardize wording to "monotonically increasing" / "monotonically 
  decreasing" across all four classes

_No response_

BinaryTree/KDTree statistics are not thread-safe (and might be a performance issue)

> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

In `BinaryTree.query()`, we have:

```python
        self.n_trims = 0
        self.n_leaves = 0
        self.n_splits = 0
```

and these are incremented in methods called by `query()`. Since a tree can be simultaneously used from multiple threads:

1. The statistics will be garbage, as the numbers will get overwritten by different threads.
2. It's possible that this will slow down operation as the same memory needs to be pushed between caches across CPU cores.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import threading
import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import KDTree

samples = np.random.rand(10_000, 10)
query_points = np.random.rand(10_000, 10)
tree = KDTree(samples, 10)

def run_and_get_stats():
    tree.query(query_points, dualtree=False, breadth_first=False, sort_results=False)
    return tree.get_tree_stats()

# Single-threaded version, resets stats to zero:
print("Single threaded:")
assert run_and_get_stats() == run_and_get_stats()
print("OK")

# Threaded version:
print("Threaded:")
thread_stats = set()
threads = []
for _ in range(10):
    t = threading.Thread(target=lambda: thread_stats.add(run_and_get_stats()))
    threads.append(t)
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

assert len(thread_stats) == 1
assert thread_stats.pop() == run_and_get_stats()
print("OK")
```

### Expected Results

Running in parallel should, given the current contract, give the same results. This is not really possible.

So really the API should be changed so `query()` does _not_ reset to zero, and instead increments existing stats.

Handling of classes with all-zero weights

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

If passing multi-class data to a classifier where some class has only observations with zero weights, estimators will produce odd solutions which do not really make sense.

For example:
```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.random(size=(30, 3))
y = rng.integers(3, size=X.shape[0])
w = rng.standard_gamma(1, size=X.shape[0])
w[y == 1] = 0.

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
LogisticRegression().fit(X, y, w).coef_
```
```
array([[-0.01295201,  0.04689646, -0.19975591],
       [ 0.0006037 ,  0.00044906,  0.00039081],
       [ 0.01234832, -0.04734552,  0.19936509]])
```

Mathematically, the correct solution would be something with a minus infinite as intercept and zeros in all coefficients, and the same applies to other classifiers with intercepts (e.g. gradient boosters), but I don't think this would be a desirable solution.

Technically, the sample weights according to the documentation should be interpreted as if each observation would be repeated the amount of times given by the weights, and if we take that as zero, that means leaving them out, in which case the classes with zero weights would be removed during the pre-processing and would not be available under `model.classes_`.

But that sort of behavior would be quite problematic for other libraries that aim at providing scikit-learn-compatible interfaces - for example, it'd contradict the docs that instruct developers to call `np.unique` to get the classes ([link](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html#estimator-types)), and if implemented in such a way that [validate_data](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.utils.validation.validate_data.html) could return something with different shape than the input, it might require other scikit-learn-compatible libraries to have a hard dependency on scikit-learn, and would likely break many things if the shapes differ.

Thus, I think the most reasonable behavior here would be to error out with an informative message.

For reference, this is what GLMNET would do, and would even have a non-zero threshold for it which is perhaps a more reasonable way of handling it:
```r
library(glmnet)
data("iris")
x <- iris[, -5]
y <- iris$Species
w <- rep(1, length(y))
w[y == "virginica"] <- 0
glmnet(x, y, weights=w, family="multinomial")
```

```

In order of preference, should either:
* Error out; or
* Filter out the classes; or
* Produce a mathematically correct solution.

### Actual Results

Prevent CPU over-subscription when using thread pools, similar to what process pools do

### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Process pools in sklearn will limit the number of threads used by OpenMP and BLAS. Thread pools will not set any limits.

Consider the following program, which lists how many threads are set for OpenMP/OpenBLAS/etc:

```python
import joblib, sys
from sklearn.utils.parallel import Parallel, delayed
import threadpoolctl

def print_thread_pool_sizes():
    for info in threadpoolctl.threadpool_info():
        print(info["user_api"], info["internal_api"], f"threads: {info['num_threads']}")

with joblib.parallel_config(backend=sys.argv[1]):
    Parallel(n_jobs=-1)([delayed(print_thread_pool_sizes)()])
```

When run under the default backend, the loky process pool, I get:

```
$ python nested-parallelism.py loky
blas openblas threads: 1
blas openblas threads: 1
openmp openmp threads: 1
```

When run under the threading joblib backend, I get:

```
$ python nested-parallelism.py threading
blas openblas threads: 20
blas openblas threads: 20
openmp openmp threads: 20
```

This can lead to significant CPU oversubscription, depending on the semantics of the library:

* When using OpenBLAS, you will get a total of 40 (20 + 20) threads, since the limit is for a single thread pool shared by the whole process.
* When using OpenMP, you will get 400 (20 * 20) threads, since the limit is _per operation starting a thread pool._

The result is code that runs slower, wasting CPU cycles, and not actually achieving any more work.

### Describe your proposed solution

There are a number of scenarios:

**Scenario 1: All cores:** If the number of threads in a thread pool is the same as the number of (available) CPU cores, setting the OpenMP/BLAS limit to 1 will work correctly: no oversubscription, no cores sitting idle.
 
**Scenario 2: All cores but 1 or 2:** If the requested number of threads/processes is negative number `-N` in joblib, this is defined as "number of available cores + 1- N". I.e. this semantically suggests the users wants to saturate the cores, but leave a few cores for other tasks. Typically N will be small, e.g. 2 to leave one core free but use all others. In this case again setting the OpenMP/BLAS limit to 1 is the right thing to do.

**Scenario 3: A hard-coded small number of cores, less than available cores:** The remaining case is most likely when the number of cores is limited due to the way the algorithm works. For process pools joblib will already automatically set the number of threads in OpenMP/BLAS to `max(cpu_count() // effective_n_jobs, 1)`. So for example if you have 10 cores and only starting a pool of size 5, OpenMP/BLAS will each be set to allow 2 threads. In a process pool, this works fine.

For a top-level thread pool, this heuristic works fine for OpenMP but _not_ OpenBLAS, since the meaning of "2" is different: for OpenMP it means "2 threads for every operation started in the 5 threads, for a total of 2 * 5 == 10 threads", for OpenBLAS it means "2 threads for the whole process, for a total of 5 + 2 threads."

So this suggests two options; one could choose one, the other, or both:

1. Documentation for algorithms with limited parallelism, suggesting that it's better to use processes in order to utilize all cores.
2. Custom settings per parallelism mechanism: set OpenMP to `max(cpu_count() // effective_n_jobs, 1)` and BLAS to `cpu_count()`. This could still lead to oversaturation in certain edge cases, but perhaps it's not as bad. 

> As a follow-up it looks like MKL at least can due OpenMP-style configuration, with a different API than the one `threadpoolctl` uses.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

This could be implemented in joblib, rather than in sklearn, but that's a more generic context; there are additional threaded libraries that it might grow support for over time, whereas sklearn has more restricted set. Still, this arguably also be done as the default joblib policy for thread pools.

### Additional context

`joblib.cpu_count()` is aware of CPU resource constraints when running inside Linux containers, so its notion of "all available cores" is usually quite accurate.

I am happy to implement this.

I have also tested this [on actual code](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/auto_examples/compose/plot_compare_reduction.html), and `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1` on an all-cores thread pool makes the resulting calculation run faster and reduce involuntary context switches. This is not a perfect experiment since OpenBLAS in threaded mode is often _slower_ than single-threaded OpenBLAS for small tasks, so a better experiment would be with some code that uses OpenMP, if someone can suggest one.
